name: Kalighat Painting Workshop
description: KALIGHAT PAINTINGS – WHERE TRADITION MEETS MODERNITYBengal is renowned for its rich cultural heritage and diverse artistic traditions, including music, literature, dance, and visual arts. In this workshop, we will explore one of Bengal's most fascinating and thought-provoking art forms—Kalighat Paintings.Bold, expressive & vibrant, Kalighat paintings beautifully bring together a variety of themes, ranging from Hindu mythology and spirituality to secular life and social commentary.Originating in 19th-century Kolkata during the colonial period, this distinctive art form developed around the Kalighat Temple, dedicated to Goddess Kali. The paintings were traditionally created on patas (cloth or paper scrolls) by artists known as Patuas. Located near the banks of the Hooghly River and the popular Kalighat Temple, the area attracted pilgrims, locals, and foreign visitors, creating a thriving audience for these unique artworks.However, with the growing popularity of printed reproductions in the early 20th century, traditional handmade Kalighat paintings gradually declined.The legacy of this expressive art form was later reinterpreted and celebrated by renowned Indian artist Jamini Roy, who drew inspiration from Bengal's folk traditions and brought a distinctive modern interpretation to traditional Indian art.What will you learn?Learn about the history and evolution of Kalighat PaintingsExplore the life and artistic journey of Jamini RoyUnderstand the distinctive themes, styles, and visual language of this art formDiscover how traditional Indian folk art influenced modern artistic expressionCreate your very own Kalighat-inspired paintingThis will be a wonderful opportunity to experience Indian art and culture through storytelling, learning, and hands-on creativity!Note:All art materials required for the workshop will be provided by the host.What will you take home?A Detailed Hands-On Workshop WorkbookKnowledge & History of Kalighat art & cultureYour very own completed artwork created during the workshopWhat do you need to bring?A water bottle to keep yourself hydrated.All workshop materials will be provided. However, if preferred, you may bring an examination pad or paper board for additional support while working.Please NoteKindly be on time, Participants arriving late may miss the storytelling and introduction to the history of this beautiful art form.No refunds will be provided for cancellations.Come, explore the vibrant world of Kalighat Paintings, where storytelling, tradition, culture, and creativity come together & take home a beautiful piece of art created by you!

description: Shoonya — emptiness, the zero, the point past which nothing further needs saying — is where this evening is headed. Rather than build to a peak, this is a night that quietens, note by note, until only stillness remains.Vedanth Bharadwaj and Gurupriya Atreya begin. They start with the Bhakti poets, songs that still have some movement and argument in them, lullabies from across the world and then turn gradually towards gentler pieces, the kind that ask the room to lean in rather than sit back.Mir Rajak and Group follow, Mirasi musicians from Pugal in Rajasthan, whose families have sung the Sufiyana kalam for generations. Their music is often full-throated, built for courtyards and long nights. Tonight they sing Kabir, Bulleh Shah and other Sufi poets in its softer, more inward register, the way these songs are sung when the gathering is small and no one is in a hurry.By the end, if it works, the last note will not feel like a finish. It will feel like the room has simply gone quiet.

name: आज रंग है - Aaj Rang Hai
description: Aaj Rang HaiThere is a folk tale in Chishti circles about Amir Khusrau. He goes looking for a guru, finds Nizamuddin Auliya, and what comes out of him isn't a treatise but a song: aaj rang hai, today there is colour. Whether it happened quite like that, no one can say. But the song has been sung at the dargah in Delhi for about seven hundred years, and singers still turn to it when they want to name the moment when searching stops and something simply arrives.This evening's three sets come from three corners of the country, and from three different ways of living with that same question.Gurupriya Atreya and Vedanth Bharadwaj open with Kabir and the other Bhakti poets. Vedanth trained in Carnatic, Hindustani and Western classical music, and for years has sung the saint-poets, Bhakti and Sufi alike. Gurupriya sings with him. These verses were never meant to sit on a page. They were made to be sung among people, and that is how the two of them take them up.Santhi Priya follows with songs of the Bauls. For generations the Bauls of Bengal have been wanderers, singing about the moner manush, the person of the heart, the divine who lives in the body rather than in a temple or a mosque. Santhi Priya learned this music from her guru, Parvathy Baul, and is spoken of as the first woman from Kerala to sing it. A tradition this rooted in Bengal now has a voice from the other end of the country, which says something about how these songs have always moved: on foot, from teacher to student.After a short break, Mir Rajak and Group come to us from Pugal in Rajasthan. They are Mirasis, a hereditary community of musicians whose families have carried the Sufiyana kalam for centuries. In a single sitting they will go from Bulleh Shah and Khwaja Ghulam Farid to the bhajans of Kabir and Meera, without pausing to mark the change. For them there is no border to cross. The labels we bring, Sufi here and Bhakti there, are mostly our own.

name: Workshop - चलो हमारा देस - Chalo Hamara Des
description: Chalo hamara des, come to my country, is one of Kabir's recurring calls. The country he means is not on any map. It is his name for the place a seeker arrives at when the searching quiets down, and in the oral traditions of Malwa and elsewhere, singers have carried this invitation from village to village for centuries, mostly in the voices of people who never thought of themselves as performers.This workshop takes that call as its starting point. Over four and a half hours, we will learn and sing songs from Kabir, Meerabai and the Sufi kalam, and pay attention to what they are actually saying. Many of these songs begin with ordinary things: a pot, a thread, a well, a lamp, a road. From there they move, sometimes in a single line, towards what cannot be seen or named. We will follow that movement, starting with the familiar and letting the songs take us further in.The poets did not agree on one way of walking this road. Meera longs and waits. Kabir argues, mocks and asks awkward questions. The Sufis speak of remembrance, of surrender, of the beloved. We will spend time with each of these voices, and notice where they meet.You do not need to have sung before. These songs were made to be sung together, by people sitting on the ground, not by trained voices on a stage. What matters here is listening closely and joining in.

name: An Immersive Workshop - Jo Dooba So Paar
description: An immersive workshop with  Artists Vedanth Bharadwaj and Mir Rajak and team , its a musical journey into surrender through the songs of Meerabai, Kabir, and Sufi mystics.Jo Dooba So Paar is an invitation to surrender—to step beyond the instinct to hold on, control, and understand, and to discover what becomes possible when we allow ourselves to be carried by the song.The phrase carries a beautiful paradox. In ordinary life, we learn to keep ourselves afloat—to hold on to certainty, identity, control, and the familiar. But in the songs of mystics, surrender can become another kind of crossing. When the grip loosens, something deeper can reveal itself.Across the Bhakti and Sufi traditions, the language of drowning is not one of defeat. To drown is to let the separate self loosen its grip; to cross is to discover another shore. In this paradox lies the heart of the workshop: perhaps the way across is not through resistance, but through surrender.Through songs, poetry, collective singing and deep listening, we will explore longing, love, devotion, dissolution and the mysterious movement from 'I' towards something larger than oneself.Drawing from Kabir and Meerabai and Sufi saints, the workshop brings together diverse musical traditions that speak, in different voices, of the same inward movement.Sometimes, the shore is found only when we stop trying to stay afloat.Jo Dooba So Paar is an invitation to take that leap: to enter the song deeply enough that, for a moment, there is no need to know where we are going.Perhaps that is the mystery of the mystic's path—the one who dares to drown discovers that the other shore was never far away.No prior experience of singing is required. The emphasis is on listening, participation, voice and the shared experience of letting the song take us somewhere.

name: Rethinking Work in Midlife
description: From Leadership to the Boardroom: What Does It Take?After years of leading teams, building businesses and making decisions, have you ever wondered whether a board role could be part of your next chapter?Board roles and independent directorships are often seen as a natural progression for experienced professionals. It's an open, practical conversation about the possibilities and realities of board work, with time for your questions.What we'll exploreHow experienced professionals find their way into board rolesWhat changes when you move from an executive role to a board roleWhat boards look for in independent directorsThe responsibilities, risks and trade-offs involvedHow you can begin exploring this path before making a larger commitmentWho is this for?Experienced professionals, senior leaders, entrepreneurs and independent professionals who are curious about board roles and independent directorships, whether as a future possibility or something they are already beginning to explore.

name: GFT: Bangalore Lectures
description: Grounds for Thought: October 2026 (Koramangala)A Blue Tokai × unLecture SeriesGrounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. October runs across Delhi and Bangalore, moving from temple sculpture to constitutional pedagogy, from parenting in the AI age to the politics of a Bollywood item number.10th October: Pritha ChakrabartiBollywood's song-and-dance numbers get read as spectacle, or dismissed outright as objectification — rarely as historical documents. Pritha Chakrabarti, who heads the School of Film and Media Studies at Alliance University, Bengaluru, argues that Hindi cinema's item numbers and love ballads alike chart the making of a modern, and later neoliberal, India — desire, economy, gendered codes, and national imagination all playing out on screen. Drawing on a career spanning journalism, advertising, and screenwriting alongside her PhD in Cultural Studies, she asks what today's "swag" shares with yesterday's aada, and what our most exported songs reveal about who we became.24th October: Ritash (they/zey)A first-person account of being in New York on 9/11, and of the years that followed working inside the institutions whose language and instincts that day seemed only to confirm. Ritash, NeuroQueer and gender-fluid writer and co-founder of RANG Foundation, traces the tangle of capitalism, casteism, Islamophobia, queerphobia, and ableism as lived experience rather than theory — and asks what it means to keep working inside a system while never fully making peace with it.

Pritha Chakrabarti, who heads the School of Film and Media Studies at Alliance University, Bengaluru, argues that Hindi cinema's item numbers and love ballads alike chart the making of a modern, and later neoliberal, India — desire, economy, gendered codes, and national imagination all playing out on screen. Drawing on a career spanning journalism, advertising, and screenwriting alongside her PhD in Cultural Studies, she asks what today's "swag" shares with yesterday's aada, and what our most exported songs reveal about who we became.24th October: Ritash (they/zey)A first-person account of being in New York on 9/11, and of the years that followed working inside the institutions whose language and instincts that day seemed only to confirm. Ritash, NeuroQueer and gender-fluid writer and co-founder of RANG Foundation, traces the tangle of capitalism, casteism, Islamophobia, queerphobia, and ableism as lived experience rather than theory — and asks what it means to keep working inside a system while never fully making peace with it.

name: Who Gets to Adapt? Online webinar
description: Who Gets to Adapt? Gender, Care and Everyday Life in a Changing ClimateWe’re often told that adapting to climate change means changing how we live – travelling differently, staying indoors during extreme heat, finding ways to cope with flooding, conserving water, or changing our routines.But adaptation isn’t equally available to everyone.What happens when your ability to adapt is shaped by your gender, the work you do, how you move through the city, how much you earn, whether you feel safe, or the people you are responsible for caring for?And when climate disruption enters everyday life, who absorbs the extra work of making things function — changing schedules, finding water, caring for others, navigating unsafe conditions, or simply carrying on?This conversation asks a deceptively simple question: who gets to adapt?And perhaps more importantly: when we ask people to adapt to a changing climate, who is actually absorbing the cost of that adaptation?
